LESSON 65 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

Broken Access Control and IDOR

Why the identifier in a URL is caller-chosen data, how an insecure direct object reference exposes other people's records, and where the authorisation check has to sit.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Broken access control is the top category in the current OWASP list, and the reason is structural: applications grant access in many places, and any one of them being wrong is a breach. Insecure direct object reference is its most common form.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Comparing missing object-level checks (IDOR/BOLA) with server-side principal-to-resource policy enforcement.

01 Authenticated User A
GET /records/104
02 Route Handler
Allowed
03 User A Record
  1. Actor: Signed-in user clicks a link generated for their own account.
  2. Boundary: Server looks up the requested object identifier.
  3. Resource: Caller receives their own authorized data.
01 Authenticated User A
GET /records/105
02 Identity-Only Check
Unblocked
03 User B Record
  1. Actor: User A modifies the record ID in the URL, JSON body, or API call.
  2. Boundary: Handler verifies that User A is logged in, but never checks ownership of ID 105.
  3. Resource: Server returns or mutates User B's private record (horizontal breach).
01 Authenticated User A
WHERE owner_id = session.uid
02 Policy + Ownership Gate
Verified
03 403 / Scoped Query
  1. Actor: Caller requests any object identifier or privileged operation.
  2. Boundary: Centralized policy checks (principal, action, resource ownership) on the server.
  3. Resource: Unauthorized cross-account access is denied before data is read or modified.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • An access decision needs the identity, the action and the specific object, and a check that omits the object is not a check.
  • A sequential identifier in a URL is an invitation: if /invoice/41 fails, /invoice/42 probably works.
  • Correct checks are often present on the list page and missing on the detail, edit or delete endpoint.
  • Client-side hiding of a control is not enforcement, because the request can be sent directly.
  • Bulk endpoints are especially risky, because one request can act on many objects at once.

The background

  • Early applications assumed a user either saw everything or nothing, so per-object checks were rarely written.
  • The transition to many customers on one system made per-object checks necessary, and the gap was never fully closed.
  • The industry survey has ranked broken access control near the top for several editions, and it is first in the 2025 list.
  • Centralised policy and relationship-based access control are the current direction for avoiding scattered decisions.

Real-world examples

  • Changing an identifier in a URL returns another customer data, which is one of the most common serious findings in testing.
  • A delete endpoint with no ownership check lets a user remove records that are not theirs.
  • An administrative action guarded only by a hidden menu item is reachable by anyone who knows the URL.

What to look for

  • Check every endpoint that takes an object identifier and ask whether it verifies permission for that object.
  • Check whether identifiers are guessable, and whether guessing is rate-limited or detected.
  • Check whether administrative functionality is separated from ordinary functionality, not just styled differently.
  • Check whether any endpoint accepts an identifier list, since per-object checks are often skipped for bulk actions.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Default to deny and grant explicitly, so an unimplemented check fails closed rather than open.
  • Enforce the check on the server for every request, and make it part of the data access layer rather than the route.
  • Use unguessable identifiers as defence in depth, not as a replacement for a check.
  • Rate-limit and log authorisation failures, since a burst of them is a clear signal.
  • Test every endpoint with two accounts of different privilege; this finds these flaws faster than any scanner.
